questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8x-12y+1}{12x-18y+3}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-3y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4(2x-3y)+1}{6(2x-3y)+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-3y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{4z+1}{6z+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2z+1}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1}{2z+1}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2+y-x}{x-y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2-(x-y)}{x-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2(z-1)}{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{2(z-1)}{z}.$

Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x+8y-1}{4}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+4y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(x+4y)-1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+4y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+4\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1) & =\frac{2z-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2z.$

Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3x+6y.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3(x+2y).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1) & =3z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=6z+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=6z+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(5x+y)}{(5x+y)+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=5x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-5.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-5 & =\frac{2z}{z+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{7z+5}{z+1}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{7z+5}{z+1}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2{sin}^{2}⁡(3x+3y)-1.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(g(x,y))=-6x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(3(x+y))-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(3z)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2{sin}^{2}⁡(3z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{csc}^{2}⁡(3z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡(3z)\,\text{d}z & =\int 2\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3z) & =2x+K \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡(3z) & =-6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x+3y)=-6x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=3x+3y.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}+8xy+4{y}^{2}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(g(x,y))=2x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(x+y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =4{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=4{z}^{2}+1.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{4{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2z) & =x+K \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(2z) & =2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+2y)=2x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=2x+2y.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x+y}{3-2x-y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=-\frac{x+y}{3}+C
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+y}{3-(2x+y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{z}{3-z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6-z}{3-z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{3-z}{6-z})\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\frac{z-3}{z-6})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \int (\frac{3}{z-6}+1)\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡|z-6|+z & =x+K\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6|+2x+y & =x+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6| & =-\frac{x+y}{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{K}{3}.$

Therefore,

$$
g(x,y)=2x+y-6.
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+5y)-1.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=10x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5(x+y))-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5z)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡(5z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \int \operatorname{cot}⁡(5z)\,\text{d}z & =2\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5z)| & =2x+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5z)| & =10x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+5y)|=10x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+5y).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2+4{x}^{2}-4xy+{y}^{2}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2+(2x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2+{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}={z}^{2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{z} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{1}{2x-y}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2xy - x^2 - y^2.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z= x - y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form $z'(x) = f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(x-y)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = x - y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 - \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad \Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  1 - \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z),$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  =  z^2 + 1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z) = z^2 + 1.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{1 - x - y}{x + y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y) = 2x + C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-(x+y)}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 + \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{{z}^{2}}{2} & =x+K \\ {z}^{2} & =2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = 2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x+y)^2 = 2x + C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y) = (x+y)^2.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we're given a differential equation of the form

$$
y' = F(x,y).
$$

By factoring the function $F(x,y),$ we can often convert this differential equation to one that is of the form 

$$
y' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. Then, using the substitution $z= ax+by,$ we can convert the equation to a separable differential equation. 

To illustrate, let's consider the differential equation

$$
y'  = 9x^2 - 6xy + y^2.
$$

Notice that the right-hand side is a perfect square. So, we factor it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=(3x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = 3x - y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} 
\quad \Rightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

Therefore, we can write our equation in terms of $z$ as

$$
3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = z^2,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}   = 3-z^2.
$$

We now have a separable differential equation.
